before.text:
quantum chaotic system comes from Gutzwiller’s pioneering work [3], that expresses the
oscillatory part of the quantum density of states as a sum over classical periodic orbits.
(Such sums are now referred to as trace formulas.) It is well-known that the oscillatory part
of the density of the Riemann zeros is given by a Gutzwiller-like sum, with one periodic term
for every integer power of a prime number [4]. (A smoothed density of the Riemann zeros
has also been studied in Ref. [5].) From this perspective, one can infer that a spectrum
consisting of the Riemann zeros is generated by a Hamiltonian (albeit unknown) whose
classical orbits have actions that are logarithms of primes and integer powers of primes.

before.text:
largely ignored. Interestingly, it is the latter that contains the essential information about
the location of the primes, as shown below. There is a vast literature on the distribution
of the prime numbers. It is recognized that their distribution exhibits global regularity and
local irregularity [7]. The nearest-neighbour spacings (NNS) of the primes is known to be
Poisson-like [8], corresponding to an almost uncorrelated random distribution. This is very
different in character from the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble (GUE) distribution of the Rie-
mann zeros. Nevertheless, it is possible to generate the almost-uncorrelated sequence of all
integer powers of primes from the interference of the highly-correlated Riemann zeros.

before.text:
density of the Riemann zeros has the structure of a dynamical trace formula with periodic
orbits. It is natural to ask whether Riemann’s formula is a trace formula for the primes.
Despite having the oscillatory terms, as discussed below, Riemann’s formula is not a trace
formula of dynamical origin. But, this does not preclude the existence of a trace formula
for the primes. If one does exist, then this would support the notion that there exists a
Hamiltonian system whose quantum spectrum is the primes. In any case, the exclusion
of Riemann’s formula as a trace formula suggests that there would be no correspondence
between the classical dynamics and the Riemann zeros for this system.

By writing ζ(γ + it) = |ζ(γ + it)| exp(−iθγ (t)), we see that all the information about the
zeros along the t−axis is contained in the phase θγ (t). This has to jump by π to accomodate
the sign change in ζ at every zero, and it can be shown that the oscillating part of the
density of the zeros on the critical line is proportional to the derivative of the imaginry part
of ln ζ(t) with respect to t [10]. On the other hand, we see from Eq. (2) that the appropriate
contour integral over ln ζ(β) also yields ρ(x) relating to the primes. Thus, the phase of the
zeta function, as defined above, connects the Riemann zeros to the primes.

values. Although the higher frequency terms are responsible for short-range oscillations

before.text:
<!-- source-page: 13 -->

experiment is to move the zeros off the critical line, that is, to arbitrarily change their real
parts. We find this still produces lines at the primes and their powers, but the relative
intensities are incorrect. This is interesting since it demonstrates that the location of the
primes depends only on the imaginary part of the zero. The real part only affects the
intensities which are anyway not evident from a direct evaluation of the series. This provides
another motivation for the numerical and analytical procedures described in this paper.

after.text:
With regard to spectral statistics, it is well known that nearest-neighbour spacings (NNS)
[19] of the Riemann zeros obey the GUE distribution of Random Matrix Theory, character-
istic of a chaotic quantum system without time-reversal symmetry [20, 21]. The same zeros
also generate the spectrum of the primes and their powers through Riemann’s formula (3).
As mentioned earlier, the NNS distribution of the primes is Poisson-like [8], with some level
repulsion, which, if at all of dynamic origin, hints only to near-integrability [1]. Thus, it is
quite remarkable that the highly-correlated sequence of the zeros can (through Riemann’s
formula) interfere to produce the almost-uncorrelated sequence of the primes.

related_synthesis_entries.claim: Shared phase/oscillation structure gives meaningful two-way prime/zero representations, while missing orbit repetitions, index-independent amplitudes, and the trivial-zero smooth term prevent upgrading that resemblance to a Hamiltonian trace formula.
related_synthesis_entries.limit: The obstruction applies to Riemann's formula as written and does not rule out a different trace formula or Hamiltonian for the prime spectrum.

risk_spans.reason: Technical note explains that integrating only from 1 changes the small-sigma convolution insignificantly; useful qualification but not a distinct reusable mechanism.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: Smoothness does not determine dynamical provenance: the smooth contribution created by trivial zeta zeros cannot simply be relabeled as Thomas-Fermi background.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: The footnote states that the second smooth term on the right-hand side of equation (3) arises from the trivial zeros and may not be included in a Thomas-Fermi term.
directed.conceptual_reading: Components should be classified by how they arise, not only by their visual regularity. Analytic zero data and semiclassical mean-density data carry different semantics even when both are smooth in x.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The equation's smooth part must be decomposed by provenance: the trivial-zero contribution is separated from any candidate Thomas-Fermi contribution.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The note excludes one smooth term from the Thomas-Fermi interpretation; it does not prove that the remaining smooth term is generated by a Hamiltonian or repair the broader trace-formula analogy.
directed.uncertainty: Low; the caveat is explicit and independent of damaged formula layout.
